World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Tobacco ban in the UK could create smoke-free generation
World.content:
Anyone born after 2008 will be banned from buying cigarettes or vapes for life in the UK when a new bill becomes law.

The landmark legislation aims to stop anyone born on or after January 1, 2009 from taking up smoking or vaping by making it illegal to sell them tobacco products.

The bill aims to create a smoke-free generation and is part of a suite of measures aimed at tackling the health effects of smoking.

Peak bodies for health and groups that advocate for quitting tobacco say a change like this would be welcomed in Australia but much would need to be done to stamp out the thriving illegal tobacco trade first.

Here's what you need to know.

What are the proposed laws?

Under the bill, it will be illegal for anyone currently aged 17 or under to ever buy cigarettes in the UK.

The ban will come into effect on January 1, 2027.

Retailers that sell these products would be expected to enforce the rules.

The bill will also ban advertising and sponsorship of all vapes and other nicotine products, such as nicotine pouches.

The UK government says it will close loopholes and ban all vapes and nicotine products from being sold to under 18s as well as ban the free distribution of these products and their sale from vending machines.

Ministers will have the power to regulate the flavours, packaging and display of all vapes and other nicotine products, as well as to amend and update product standards.

It will make playgrounds and areas near schools and hospitals smoke-free areas, and tighten existing restrictions in workplaces.

Could a generational smoking ban happen in Australia?

In Australia, the Cancer Council's National Tobacco Issues Committee chair Alecia Brooks said it was always encouraging to see new policies internationally developed to protect new generations from taking up tobacco use.

"The United Kingdom's move to ban people born after 2008 from ever starting smoking is a significant opportunity for governments across the world to think about what the future of tobacco control may look like, particularly when it comes to protecting young people from tobacco and nicotine," she said.

Ms Brooks said there had already been major change in Australia, which had curbed smoking rates, particularly with recent laws to restrict the sale of vapes outside of a pharmacy environment.

"National data shows that the number of 14 to 17-year-olds who have never vaped has increased to 85 per cent compared to 82 per cent in early 2023.

"Additionally, data also shows that young people in 2025 who have never smoked is at its highest ever level at 94 per cent."

Ms Brooks said smoking prevalence in Australia had almost halved over the past 25 years.

Illicit tobacco laws ranked in new report The Northern Territory has been ranked last in the country for how it tackles cheap, illicit tobacco.

"This was achieved through world-class tobacco control measures that decreased the affordability, appeal, supply, access and promotion of tobacco products, which continue to decrease smoking rates and address nicotine addiction to save lives."

As restrictions on nicotine access have tightened, the illegal tobacco trade has expanded, especially over the past five years.

The Australian Council on Smoking and Health (ACOSH) released a report ranking each state and territory's response to tackling the issue.

It found the Northern Territory was the worst jurisdiction but all had room to improve.

"While we would support measures like those proposed in the UK, the immediate priority in Australia is tackling the illegal market and reducing the widespread availability of cheap tobacco," CEO of ACOSH Laura Hunter said.

"A policy like this could work here but only if it is part of a comprehensive system.

"That means not just legislation, but strong enforcement, national coordination, and sustained investment in quitting support."

A report by Australia's Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner, released last year, found illegal tobacco made up more than half of the country's tobacco market.

Ms Hunter said if legislation like this was introduced, the government would need to strengthen supply chain controls.

"If governments introduce stronger restrictions without strengthening supply chain controls, penalties, and enforcement capability, while also funding measures to reduce demand, there's a risk illegal trade will fill the gap," she said.

"We need every jurisdiction to strengthen laws to tackle the illicit tobacco trade, closure orders to shut down illegal operators, tough penalties to deter organised crime, powers for landlords to terminate leases, and consequences for landlords who turn a blind eye."

Have laws like this been implemented elsewhere?

The first nation that was set to implement a generational ban on smoking was New Zealand but the laws were repealed before implementation.

The raft of measures, which were meant to begin in July 2024, would have seen bans on selling tobacco to anyone born after January 1, 2009.

It would have also reduced the amount of nicotine allowed in smoked tobacco products and cut the number of retailers able to sell tobacco by more than 90 per cent.

The centre-right government that took power in 2023 said the former government's measures would have significantly reduced tax revenues.

But Ms Hunter believes the New Zealand government "backflipped" "because of tobacco industry interference".

"We need to ensure that tobacco industry plays no role in shaping public health policy designed to protect Australians from these deadly tobacco industry products."

The Maldives is the first and only nation that has implemented a generational smoking ban.

The Archipelago nation bans anyone born after January 1, 2007 from buying, using or being sold tobacco products.

The measure also applies to visitors.

Selling tobacco products to an underage person carries a penalty of 50,000 rufiyaa ($3,200), while using vape devices carries a fine of 5,000 rufiyaa ($320).

Where is the bill at in UK parliament?

The bill is in its final stages and it is ready to receive Royal Assent.

In UK parliament, Royal Assent is when the monarch gives it final approval so it can officially be made into law.

While the monarch has the right to refuse Royal Assent, nowadays this does not happen; the last such occasion was in 1708, and Royal Assent is regarded today as a formality.

So, essentially, the bill will become law.

World.title: Ben Roberts-Smith confirms Anzac Day plans
World.content:
Ben Roberts-Smith has confirmed he will be attending Anzac Day services tomorrow, saying he intends to pay his respects, one week on from his release on bail.

He also said he and his family have no involvement in a rally calling for the withdrawal of charges against him, planned in Melbourne for this weekend by an ethno-nationalist group.

Mr Roberts-Smith has been residing in Queensland since he was released from Sydney's Silverwater jail to await trial for five counts of the war crime of murder.

He has strenuously denied the allegations, which stem from alleged actions during his service in Afghanistan.

In a statement, he responded to supportive comments made by his fellow Victoria Cross recipient, Vietnam war veteran Keith Payne, who told The Australian newspaper: "Of course he should march or be at the Dawn Service, whatever he wants to".

"I greatly appreciate the support from Keith Payne VC and everyone else that has made contact," Mr Roberts-Smith said.

" Anzac Day is sacred to me and every other veteran. I will be attending to pay my respects and I encourage everyone else to. "

A representative for the former soldier did not say which events he would be participating in.

Ben Roberts-Smith was charged with war crimes earlier this month. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

A spokesperson for RSL Australia said all Australians, including Mr Roberts-Smith, were able to attend Anzac Day commemorations.

"As a service veteran, and like any member of the community, Ben Roberts-Smith is able to attend Anzac Day commemorations should he so choose," they said.

"RSL Australia is encouraging all Australians to come together this Anzac Day to honour the service and sacrifice of past and present veterans, and to recognise that the Anzac Spirit continues to shape the nation today."

Police feared Roberts-Smith overseas move Police were concerned war veteran Ben Roberts-Smith was attempting to move overseas and possibly to Singapore or Spain when he was arrested at Sydney Airport over war crimes allegations, court documents reveal.

RSL Australia national president Peter Tinley added: "Our responsibility is not only to honour the fallen, but to fiercely advocate for and support the living."

A rally in support of the Victoria Cross recipient is being held in Melbourne over the weekend, although Mr Roberts-Smith said he had no involvement in the event.

It is being promoted by the the National Workers Alliance, an ethno-nationalist group that claims it supports the "preservation of Western culture and identity".

Mr Roberts-Smith's lawyers said in the statement to the ABC: "Mr Roberts-Smith and his family are not in any way involved in this rally, nor associated with its organisers, and have not been consulted by the group in question."

World.title: From the WA bush to the jungle of Vietnam
World.content:
Graham Taylor turned 19 just four days before the aircraft carrier took him and fellow infantry from the 4th Battalion to the Vietnam theatre of war.

The jungle was a long way from home for the Yamatji man from Western Australia's Midwest.

He spent months in the most dangerous position of forward scout before his Commander moved him to the "safer" role of medic.

It was during this time he helped patch up 16 of his 24 platoon members who were injured in a mortar attack.

Graham Taylor (second on the left) and part of his platoon serving in Vietnam in 1971. (Supplied: Graham Taylor)

"We could hear the mortar leaving the tube but we didn't know where they were coming from, because the jungle where we were was a bit thick and we had to just wait and hope that they don't land on us," he said.

"But we did have, well, a few mortars landed in front of me, behind me, on the side.

" I was pretty lucky, I think, because the blokes who got wounded, I had to jump up, grab them, patch them up and put them somewhere safe so that the helicopter can come and pick them up eventually, you know, when everything's quietened down. "

Rural upbringing

Mr Taylor said skills he learnt growing up in rural areas including Coorow, Carnamah, Three Springs, Mount Magnet and Geraldton helped prepare him for the tough environment of Vietnam.

"We [my family] were battling and we had to go and shoot kangaroos and catch rabbits and shoot galahs and parrots and pigeons out on the farm and also when we shifted into town," he said.

It was a desire to travel that saw him 

"I wanted to see the rest of Australia and the best way of seeing Australia would have been in the military, so that's why I joined the army," he said.

Mr Taylor trained at Kapooka and Ingleburn in NSW and Townsville in Queensland before shipping out.

He could not phone home before sailing as the family did not have one. He was given a week off to travel home and say goodbye.

Graham Taylor, far right, says those left of his platoon still meet when they can. (Supplied: Graham Taylor)

"My mum, she was definitely sad to find out that I was going away," he said.

Despite the training and the 11-day voyage from Townsville, Mr Taylor said it was still a shock to arrive in the jungle.

"We went ashore on the barges, and then helicopters, Chinooks," he said.

"They were big double-rotor helicopters that carry troops … about 30 at a time, went in the helicopters and we went to Nui Dat, which is our military base, and we found our tents and that was it," he said.

" Our platoon sergeant said, 'well, you're at war now, boys and that's it, watch out' so we was ready from day one. "

Loading...

Brothers in arms

Mr Taylor described his platoon as the "United Nations" with another five Indigenous men and others originally born in England, Ireland and even Holland.

"All the men in our platoon, we all joined together, moulded together as one unit, and we became like brothers, you know, and we still are," he said.

Despite being spread out across the country, the remaining men still come together when they can.

Later this year they will reunite to mark the anniversary of the mortar attack that badly injured so many.

"It was lucky no-one died, but a few were seriously injured and they were sent home to Australia," he said.

"I've been, well I still are, friends with them for life because we are brothers in arms."

No welcome home

Mr Taylor said there was no-one at the airport welcoming the returned soldiers home to Perth.

"When we landed, we just got out," he said.

"No one was there to meet us. Well, we didn't want any commotion or anything."

At the time of the Vietnam War, a heated debate raged over whether Australia should have joined the United States in engaging in the conflict.

There were protests against Australia's involvement and veterans have described being shunned by the community and even some RSL sub-branches when they returned home.

After a break following seven months' service in Vietnam, Mr Taylor continued to serve in the army for a total of six years.

He was able to fulfil his dream of travel during time off from the Butterworth base in Malaya.

Graham Taylor says he wears his service medals with pride. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Natasha Harradine)

Now, when ANZAC and Remembrance Day comes along, Mr Taylor said to be able to wear his war medals "means a great deal".

"I feel so proud because it is funny, when I was a kid going to school, I remember seeing a Second World War veteran and a Korean War veteran wearing their medals at school," he said.

"I was thinking, 'gee, I wonder if I'll be able to wear something like that one day'.

"I never thought anything of it until I'm here now today wearing medals that tells everyone that I've been overseas, you know, serving for this country."

World.title: Want to buy a football team? Why this club's next chapter is unwritten
World.content:
The tale of Canberra United FC facing a precarious outlook is so familiar that news of the club's financial woes might not capture interest.

But leagues of local football fans, and the league's all-time top scorer, would implore you to prick up your ears.

"As a group, as a player, we are not just going to be waiting around like we did last year," club captain Michelle Heyman said.

" This is our profession, this is our careers that people are toying with. "

Canberra United FC is the A-League Women's only stand-alone team, but it also has no owner, resulting in an unwritten next chapter.

Over the past few seasons, players have been limited to one-year contracts due to the uncertainty.

The club has been saved a few times, but was given one final lifeline last year when the ACT government gave Capital Football $800,000 — half of which has been used for this season.

Michelle Heyman says the uncertainty is appalling at a professional club. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Capital Football is responsible for running football in the ACT, but unlike other state and territory-based organisations, it runs a professional side — putting a strain on its resources.

The club's financial uncertainty comes as United prepares to play its first finals game at McKellar Park in a decade — taking on last year's finalists, Melbourne Victory.

How did we get here?

Ahead of the 2021-22 season, the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) then-chief executive Danny Townsend announced an expansion of the women's competition.

The W-League was rebranded to A-League Women's, with the Wellington Phoenix joining, followed by Western United in the next season.

The inclusion of new teams meant more games and more financial requirements.

Unlike other clubs, which have private ownership and resources, the growth has pushed Capital Football to the financial brink.

United is a nod to the past, and maybe a relic of it, as the other foundation clubs transitioned to a private ownership model, Canberra remained tied to its grassroots.

Michelle Heyman of Canberra United is a striker for the Matildas. (Getty Images: Aryanna Frank/USSF)

What would the loss of Canberra United FC mean?

The departure of United would mean the competition would have lost two clubs in successive years, after the departure of Western United this season.

It's a situation Professional Footballers Australia (PFA) chief executive Beau Busch doesn't want to repeat.

"Western United was incredibly traumatic for players [and] for fans," Busch said.

"We need to avoid any repeats around that. It can't happen again.

"We can't be having these same sorts of discussions … and the uncertainty on that at the same time as trying to build the league."

Beau Busch says the league needs to avoid repeating the loss of Western United. (Supplied)

Last season, there were 284 contracted professional, scholarship, and youth players in the competition — with clubs required to have a minimum of 18 professional players per squad, and a maximum of 23.

If they were to lose another club next year, assuming Western United cannot return, nearly 15 per cent of the places for female footballers in the top-flight would have been lost in just two years.

It could leave many with limited opportunity to break through or force them to move overseas for other opportunities.

APL chief executive Steve Rosich said Canberra is a priority market for the league, and it remains in regular contact with both Capital Football and the ACT government.

"We're engaged in meaningful and current discussions with multiple potential partners as we proactively pursue a new, long-term owner for the club," Mr Rosich said.

The league has not announced whether it will step in to save Canberra, as it has previously done for clubs in the A-League Men's, including the Central Coast Mariners, Newcastle Jets, and Perth Glory.

Massive Matildas hype hasn't translated to A-League Women fandom Despite the recent hype of the Matildas, support for the A-League Women remains relatively low.

Why isn't the Matildas' success translating?

So how can a country that has seen the Matildas explode in popularity, revenue and public awareness have a failing domestic women's competition?

The blame can be shared between past operators, Football Australia, the current owners of the APL, and the space in which football exists in the public consciousness.

Both past and present administrators have failed to convert national team fans and fans of European teams into domestic fans.

Some fans have blamed the accessibility of venues, the broadcast and the overall visibility of the A-League Women.

The PFA believes that it can be changed with greater investment in the league and a turn to full-time professionalism in the women's game.

Canberra United fan Brydie (right) says the thought of the team leaving the competition is not something she wants to face. (ABC News)

It's a belief that Canberra United fans Hugo and Brydie share.

"Women's sport has the ability to be a stand-alone success; we are seeing that with the Matildas, but also internationally," Brydie said.

"We are seeing so many women's teams have so much success economically, but not in terms of community support."

As a fan of Canberra United since childhood, the thought of the club leaving the competition is something Brydie doesn't want to face.

"The thought of not having that is really scary and not something I have grappled with yet, just because I'm so scared of that future and hopeful that something is going to happen," she said.

Club captain Heyman said she is staying focused on what she can control.

"The biggest way to do it is to continue to win," Heyman said.

"It would be hard to knock a team down if you win the league."

World.title: Pentagon awards $276m AUKUS contract funded by Australia
World.content:
The Pentagon has awarded the first major submarine contract to deliver on the AUKUS security deal.

The $US197 million ($276 million) contract will be covered by the Australian government's payment of $US3 billion, made to the US under AUKUS.

The contract is for engineering and design work to support the transfer of nuclear-powered submarine capabilities from the US to Australia.

The announcement came shortly after the ABC reported a critical construction contract for the submarines had been delayed despite an urgent need to fast-track their construction.

Australia intends to buy several second-hand Virginia-class submarines from the US in the 2030s.

But the deal stipulates the US will only sell the submarines, likely second-hand, if it has built enough boats to replenish the American fleet.

Australia has six Collins-class submarines (pictured), which are to be replaced by nuclear-powered vessels under AUKUS. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

The US Navy is aiming to almost double the pace of construction, to 2.33 boats per year, to achieve that.

But research presented to Congress this week said the pace of production had slowed to 1.1 boats per year. Construction delays increased slightly in the past year "despite substantial investments to reduce them".

The newly announced contract, which is unrelated to the unsigned construction contract, has been awarded to General Dynamics Electric Boat, a major navy contractor that builds submarines at shipyards in Connecticut.

The company aims to employ 4,600 additional workers at its Groton, Connecticut shipyard this year to tackle production backlogs as the US increases investment in shipbuilding.

The contract includes options that could take its cumulative value to $US930 million ($1.3 billion), the US Defense Department said.

The AUKUS pact has been discussed at several congressional hearings in Washington this week.

The US Navy's Indo-Pacific commander, Admiral Samuel Paparo, told one hearing that Australia was equipped to start hosting Virginia-class submarines immediately thanks to successful upgrade work at HMAS Stirling near Perth.

"From the capability that they have … we could move submarines to Stirling today," he said.

Joe Courtney says the new contract shows AUKUS "is tangibly moving forward". (ABC News: Bradley McLennan)

The US is due to start rotating American submarines through the base next year.

Under AUKUS, Australia eventually plans to build five submarines in South Australia, using US technology and parts made in Britain. The first of those are due for delivery to the Australian navy in the early 2040s.

Democratic congressman Joe Courtney, who represents Connecticut and has long been involved in the AUKUS pact, said the program was "tangibly moving forward".

"These funds … are proof that AUKUS is not just a plan on whiteboards," he said.

World.title: Arsons at licensed venues continue to baffle Victoria Police
World.content:
Police say they are yet to identify a motive behind a series of arson attacks on licensed venues in Melbourne in recent weeks.

Several restaurants and clubs in inner-Melbourne suburbs have been targeted by arsonists, but investigators say none of the owner of the venues have reported extortion threats.

South Yarra restaurant France-Soir was the latest venue to be targeted earlier this week.

Detective Inspector Chris Murray from the Arson and Explosives Squad told ABC Radio Melbourne a suspected arson attempt on the restaurant was thwarted when passers-by noticed the alleged would-be offenders.

"They saw two individuals loitering near the premises, saw a jerry can in the back and called it in," he said.

The restaurant's owner, Jean-Paul Prunetti, said he did not know why his establishment was targeted.

"We were a bit shocked because I never thought it would happen to us, but it just happened and that's it," he said.

" We're not really understanding what happened really. "

Police have charged a 31-year-old Sandringham man and a 22-year-old Mooroolbark woman with offences including possessing an imitation firearm, drug possession and using fraudulent registration plates.

Police arrested two people in relation to a fire at a Southbank bar last week. (ABC News)

Investigators are at a loss to explain the recent spate of arson attempts, saying extortion was "a logical assumption", but there was no evidence yet to back up that theory.

"Each and every owner who's been subject to an arson attack and attempted arson state they haven't been extorted, which is puzzling," Detective Inspector Murray said.

" The motive is unclear and we're trying to understand what that motive is but the owners have been very co-operative and say they haven't been threatened. "

Chris Murray, from the Arson and Explosives Squad, says police are still trying to establish a motive. (ABC News)

Investigators say several arrests they have made have helped them identify a common thread linking the arson attacks.

"What we do see is youth are being tasked to carry out these arson attacks, which is very similar to tobacco arsons," Detective Inspector Murray said.

"We're seeing them paid a few hundred bucks to a thousand-odd dollars."

Investigators urged anyone who saw suspicious behaviour near licensed venues, particularly in the early hours, to contact police.

World.title: US soldier charged with making $560,000 on Maduro removal bets
World.content:
A US Army soldier involved in the capture of Nicolás Maduro has been charged with making $US400,000 ($560,000) by betting on the removal of the ousted Venezuelan leader, the Department of Justice said.

In the weeks leading up to Mr Maduro's January 3 capture, Gannon Ken Van Dyke, a master sergeant with US Army Special Forces, used sensitive classified information to make wagers on prediction market Polymarket.

His bets were that US forces would enter Venezuela and that Mr Maduro would soon be out of power.

Trump's attack on Venezuela has been months in the making While Mr Maduro remained publicly defiant in the face of US pressure to step down, in private he was taking measures to dodge a potential US strike.

A grand jury in Manhattan federal court indicted Master Sergeant Van Dyke, 38, on charges of unlawful use of confidential government information for personal gain, theft of non-public government information, commodities fraud, wire fraud, and making an unlawful monetary transaction.

The case appeared to mark the first time the department had brought insider trading charges involving a prediction market.

"Our men and women in uniform are trusted with classified information in order to accomplish their mission as safely and effectively as possible, and are prohibited from using this highly sensitive information for personal financial gain," Acting US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

"Today's announcement makes clear no-one is above the law, and this FBI will do whatever it takes to defend the homeland and safeguard our nation's secrets," said FBI Director Kash Patel.

" Any clearance holders thinking of cashing in their access and knowledge for personal gain will be held accountable. "

The Venezuelan president was captured on January 3. (Reuters: Adam Gray)

Polymarket cooperating with investigation

Master Sergeant Van Dyke is expected to be presented before a judge in North Carolina later on Thursday, local time, the Justice Department said.

Asked by reporters about the arrest, President Donald Trump said he was not familiar with the case but that it reminded him of Pete Rose, who was banned from Major League Baseball over a gambling scandal.

"That's like Pete Rose betting on his own team," Mr Trump said.

"If he bet against his team, that would be no good, but he bet on his own team. I'll look into it."

In a post on X, Polymarket said it had referred the matter to the Justice Department. "Insider trading has no place on Polymarket. Today's arrest is proof the system works," the post read.

The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission also brought civil charges against the master sergeant.

He has been an active-duty soldier in the US Army since 2008 and had most recently been stationed at Fort Bragg in North Carolina, according to the indictment.

Armed groups may risk the US plan to control Venezuela The US plan to "recover" Venezuela could spark a domestic backlash in a country that is already heavily divided.

Prosecutors said Master Sergeant Van Dyke was involved in the "planning and execution" of the Maduro capture, but did not go into detail.

The indictment made note of a photograph he uploaded to his Google account in the early morning of January 3, hours after the US military brought Mr Maduro to the USS Iwo Jima amphibious assault ship.

"That photograph depicts Van Dyke on what appears to be the deck of a ship at sea, at sunrise wearing US military fatigues, and carrying a rifle, standing alongside three other individuals wearing US military fatigues," the indictment read.

A statement from the Justice Department said the soldier allegedly "sent most of his proceeds to a foreign cryptocurrency vault before depositing them into a newly created online brokerage account".

"Van Dyke withdrew the majority of his allegedly unlawful proceeds from his Polymarket account," the statement said.

It also said he "then took steps to conceal his identity as the trader in the Maduro- and Venezuela-related markets".

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Bush community bands together to keep century-old tradition alive
World.content:
Slumped together in a horse stable, Liz Soames has one thing on her mind.

"I'd like to wash Eidsvold out of my hair — I need a long hot shower hands down," she said.

Emma Masters, Liz Somes and Julie Stenhause won a joint award for best drover of the cattle drive. (ABC News: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ms Soames had been in the saddle driving cattle along an old stock route for a week with her best mates Emma Master and Julie Stenhouse.

Mustering about 500 beasts in the Eidsvold Cattle Drive, five hours north of Brisbane, was hard going.

The drovers prepare their horses at Eidsvold Station on the final morning of the cattle drive. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Ms Stenhouse said she hoped the girls didn't hold her 50th birthday plans against her.

"So that's why we're here; I think the girls still like me," Ms Stenhouse said.

Loading...

Ms Soames had travelled from Brisbane to take part in one of Australia's last surviving cattle drives.

Now in its 10th year, the biennial Eidsvold Cattle Drive retraces the stock routes blazed through the Queensland bush more than a century ago.

Local suppliers donated 40 dozen eggs and 40 kilograms of bacon for the cattle drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ms Soames and her two friends of more than 20 years were among the 30 participants this year.

The herd is driven down the Burnett River for the final leg of the drive to Eidsvold. (ABC News: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ms Masters said their close friendship and mutual love of horses drew them to the cattle drive.

The drovers lead 450 head of cattle along historic stockman's routes. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

"Little girls dream about horses, I never grew out of it," she said.

Ms Soames said the group of participants bonded during the week-long journey.

Local graziers donated about 450 head of cattle to the drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

"You put a whole bunch of people from different walks of life in the same place, you've got to get along, you've got to work together," she said.

"Good people skills, if you didn't have them, you've got them by the end of the week."

Army veteran and Eidsvold local Rebekah Day celebrates her 57th birthday on the cattle drive. (ABC News: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Doubling of fuel costs no barrier

Eidsvold resident Rebekah Watt celebrated her 57th birthday on the drive through the North Burnett.

"This is the best. I'm with my best friend, on a horse, in the country," Ms Watt said.

"Life is good."

Rebecca Scholl says LifeFlight and RFDS were chosen as beneficiaries. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

The army veteran reflected on the spirit of the tight-knit community that pulled together to save this year's cattle drive.

Fuel costs doubled in March, prompting organisers to hold an emergency meeting to discuss whether to go ahead.

Graham Pott and Josie Scholl are the lead drovers for the cattle drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

The following day, locals donated $5,000 and a 200-litre fuel pod, used to power the drive's bus and generators, to pull the drive back from the brink of cancellation.

About 40 volunteers supported 30 paid participants in the 2026 Eidsvold cattle drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

All proceeds from the drive will be donated to health services crucial to the region, including Lifeflight and the Royal Flying Doctor Service.

"This community is just so solid," Ms Day said.

"We've had floods and fires and all those things happen.

"The community itself, everyone pitches in and it's just phenomenal. I love living here."

About 240 people gather to celebrate the final night of the cattle drive at historic Eidsvold Station. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

'You won't see us sit around and whinge'

At the dinner that evening at Eidsvold Station, local butcher Mick Kerr took a break from cooking a roast dinner for 240 people over a campfire.

A busload of people from around the North Burnett had joined the drive's drovers and volunteers to celebrate the completion of the drive the following day.

Mundubbera butcher Mick Kerr is the camp cook for the cattle drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Mr Kerr donated 11 beef rumps for the dinner along with 40kg of bacon, 70kg of sausages and $7,500 cash to the cattle drive.

"She's a bit of a mission but yeah, I love it every bit of it," he said.

Mick Kerr donated and cooked 11 beef rumps for guests at the cattle drive's final dinner. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

He said the town was determined to see the event go ahead.

"One thing you won't see, you won't see us sit around and whinge," Mr Kerr said.

"If we've got to sort it ourselves, that's what we'll do. When an event like this is on, everyone pulls together, they make it happen and we have the best time we can."

Ros Dare travelled 1,400km to take part in the cattle drive. (ABC News: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ros Dare travelled 1,400km from the NSW town of Shellharbour to take part in the cattle drive.

She said she would spend about $1,800 on diesel, but was more concerned about the availability of fuel.

"Worst-case scenario, we could ride along the freeway, and I'd probably get lots of cheers and beeps because everybody would have known why I was riding and not driving," Ms Dare said.

Drovers and cattle enter Eidsvold on April 18. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ms Stenhouse said she needed a few nights' sleep in her own bed before making any decisions about joining the next cattle drive in 2028.

"Ask me again in a year, it might take 12 months to recover," she said.

The drovers guide the 450-strong herd into Eidsvold to complete the drive. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

"I think just that achievement of completing it is really satisfying."

A horse-drawn dray enters Eidsvold showground on the final day of the drive, Saturday April 18. (ABC Wide Bay: Olivia Nunes-Malek)

Ms Soames hoped the iconic cattle drive would continue for many years to come.

"If communities like Eidsvold didn't do this, people like us would never get to experience this," she said.

"It's just something quite unique and amazing, I really hope that it continues because you just can't get it anywhere else."

World.title: Classical Greek set to be lone odyssey for eager Victorian students
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation Classical Greek set to be lone odyssey for eager Victorian students Caroline Schelle April 24, 2026 — 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

For Victorian pupils eager to study classical Greek, the path forward is a lone odyssey through the wine-dark sea, as one of the state’s final strongholds of the subject is closing its books after nearly 150 years. Xavier College in Kew confirmed this week it will end its 147-year tradition of offering the subject due to low enrolments, but insisted it would leave the door open for future students. From left: Atticus Iliou Horn, 14, Zoe Kalanis, 15, and Peter Sofiadellis, 14, all study classical Greek and were hoping to continue it into VCE, but the subject is now at risk of being dropped. PENNY STEPHENS “While Xavier has a long history of teaching classical Greek, enrolments have not been historically consistent,” a spokesman for the school confirmed to The Age. Though the four Xavier College students undertaking the subject in years 9 and 10 this year will not be able to study the subject at VCE level, the school insisted they “have not closed the door to classical Greek if student interest grows”.



Related Article Education Veni, vidi, VCE: How a dead language helps students get top marks Through Greek Community of Melbourne Schools, students from different years across the state are learning the subject. This includes 14-year-old Atticus Iliou Horn, who is taking classes privately through the organisation, and said he was drawn to the subject as he wanted to try something new. “I think it’s a shame it may not continue, since I really enjoy the subject,” he said. English and modern Greek have inherited many aspects of classical Greek, he added. His friends Peter Sofiadellis,14, and Zoe Kalanis, 15, agreed.



“We should motivate more students to do the subject, and whether that’s scaling or promoting the subject in better ways, taking the subject out of VCE isn’t really the answer,” Sofiadellis said. For Kalanis, studying classical Greek helps her understand her place in the world. “It’s important to understand the world we live in, and ancient Greek is super-duper helpful to understand, you know, the roots of our languages and deepen our connection to our own mother country and language,” she said. Despite being a “silent” language that no one speaks, “it’s still very much alive in what I’m saying right now”, Kalanis said. Though classic works like The Odyssey are reserved for university, high school students learn texts from Herodotus and Aristophanes.



Teacher Miltiadis Paikopoulos said it is unfortunately one of those subjects that “a lot of people assumed would be around forever … but it’s had these chronic problems” of low enrolment for a long time. According to figures from the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA), which develops and carries out the state’s curriculum and exams for year 11 and year 12 students, only three students were enrolled in classical Greek for year 12 last year, compared with seven in 2024, and 12 students in 2023. These teens love classical Greek but fear for its future. PENNY STEPHENS Paikopoulos said for the subject to survive, the VCAA needed to amend its exams and there needed to be more promotion of the benefits of the language. “The skills you learn from classical Greek, the standards that it imposes on students, they flow through to all of the other subjects,” he said.



“Studying ancient Greek text within the historical context also gives students something like an advantage of studying other VCE subjects, like ancient history,” he said. Another problem was, he believed, many students did not know the subject existed. “In other words, it’s a problem with accessibility.” The issue is further complicated by the fact that Victoria’s exam materials are shared with the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA), which has said it may discontinue courses. “If the course numbers increase above 15, the discontinuation process will pause,” the NESA website reads. However, if student enrolment numbers fall below 15, courses are expected to cease by 2030.



Related Article Education The unpopular VCE subjects that could face the axe Victoria has one of the largest subject offerings in the country, with 116 topics that students can complete as part of the Victorian Certificate of Education, including more than 45 languages. The resources required to maintain so many subjects has been identified as a major issue for the authority as part of a review into the VCAA. “Many of the challenges in the VCAA can, in part, be traced back to the complexity of managing such a large range and number of subjects, all requiring a significant base workload,” governance expert Dr Yehudi Blacher found in the report published last year. World.title: France ‘open’ to selling Australia submarines if AUKUS collapses
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAUKUS France ‘open’ to selling Australia submarines if AUKUS collapses Matthew Knott April 24, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

One of France’s top ministers says the country would be willing to sell submarines to Australia if the AUKUS pact collapses, despite the acrimony sparked by the cancellation of a $90 billion deal five years ago. The Morrison government ditched a contract with Naval Group, a shipbuilding firm majority-owned by the French government, in 2021 in favour of a plan to acquire nuclear-powered submarines with the United States and United Kingdom. French President Emmanuel Macron visiting a nuclear submarine base in Crozon, northwest France, last month. AP The move triggered a diplomatic rupture between the two nations, with France recalling its ambassador from Canberra and the then French foreign minister accusing Australia of a “stab in the back”. Australia later paid $835 million in compensation to Naval Group and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese travelled to Paris to mend ties with French President Emmanuel Macron.



Asked whether his nation would be willing to enter another submarine deal with Australia, French Trade Minister Nicolas Forissier said that France was “not looking at the past”. “We will, of course, always be ready to [pursue] any partnership that would answer to the needs of Australia because we’re friends,” he told reporters in Sydney. “We are open to develop any partnership because I think we, again, are very much like-minded. We have the same philosophy.” France’s foreign trade minister, Nicolas Forissier, speaking during a January television interview. Bloomberg Retired rear admiral Peter Briggs has called for Australia to ditch AUKUS and instead seek to acquire a fleet of 12 Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines from Naval Group.



Briggs has argued the US will not have enough spare submarines to provide any to Australia, and that it would be more cost-effective and lower risk to acquire Suffren-class submarines given they are already in service with the French navy. Related Article Exclusive

AUKUS Australia’s depending on AUKUS Virginia-class subs. The US says they’re not its priority “It offers the solution to our AUKUS problems,” he wrote in a 2024 piece for the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. A Suffren-class submarine weighs 4600 tonnes compared to 7800 tonnes for the Virginia-class boats Australia plans to acquire from the US. It carries a crew of 65 submariners compared to around 132 for a Virginia-class submarine. The Suffren-class use low-enriched uranium fuel and needs refuelling every 10 years, whereas the US and British designs use highly enriched uranium and are intended never to be refuelled.



Forissier said the topic of submarines had not come up during his discussions in Australia, and local officials insist they are fully committed to AUKUS. Admiral Samuel Paparo, the top US military commander for the Indo-Pacific, this week told congress the AUKUS plan was “on track”, even though the US needs to turbocharge its submarine production rates. Asked at a conference last month whether it was too late to abandon AUKUS is favour of a new deal, Briggs said that “it is never too late to stop a plan that is not going to bloody work”. Senior Defence Department official Hugh Jeffrey told the same conference: “Defence has been directed to pursue AUKUS and we are pursuing AUKUS and that’s our plan. I would not venture into the space about ‘Plan B’ or ‘Plan C’.”



Jeffrey said Australia would be left without any submarines to replace the ageing Collins-class boats if political leaders again change their mind, urging everyone involved to “get on with business”. “This effort under AUKUS is the fourth, by my count, attempt to replace a submarine program that we began in the 1980s. Each effort, since then, to replace it has fallen afoul of domestic politics. Are we really thinking that this should be the fourth?” he asked. “If you really want to be in a position where we have no submarines, then turn back. ” Loading Forissier is the first European trade minister to visit the country since Australia and the European Union struck a free trade deal in late March.



He said he was hopeful Australia and France would be able to work together on critical minerals so they do not become “hostages in the future”, an allusion to China’s dominance of the key components for everything from iPhones to solar panels. Related Article AUKUS ‘Headed for a train smash’: Former commander’s dire AUKUS warning As a result of the free trade agreement’s removal of tariffs on European imports, Forissier said he expected Australians to buy more champagne and French dairy products. French consumers were also becoming more open to drinking imported Australian wine, he said. Forissier said that with global trade conditions become more “violent” and uncertain, it was important for countries such as Australia and France to work together as a force for stability.



US President Donald Trump imposes tariffs but “sometimes he forgets them two days after”, he said, referring to Trump’s shortlived threat of 200 per cent tariffs on imports on French wine and champagne when Macron declined an offer to join his ‘Board of Peace’ to oversee a post-war Gaza. World.title: ‘Wow, that took a while’: After two-year delay, verdict reached on fate of 200-year-old landmark
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWHeritage ‘Wow, that took a while’: After two-year delay, verdict reached on fate of 200-year-old landmark Julie Power April 24, 2026 — 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

NSW Heritage Minister Penny Sharpe has added the 200-year-old Hunter Valley sheep station Ravensworth to the state’s heritage list, despite opposition from its owner, the coal miner Glencore, and continuing debate about its contested Indigenous history. In a statement, Sharpe acknowledged her decision had taken “much longer than the statutory deadline” of two weeks. The Heritage Council recommended the listing in late 2023. The mine operations at Ravensworth in the Hunter Valley in 2021. Janie Barrett “Sometimes decisions are complex, and it is appropriate that ministers take time to consider the many facets of an issue and talk to those involved,” she said. “I note that [Glencore] do not support the listing, and they expressed this to me in person.”



Located between Singleton and Muswellbrook in the Upper Hunter, the 450-hectare site is surrounded by open-cut coal mine properties mostly owned by Glencore, including the controversial Glendell mine to the south. Scott Franks is fighting a plan to turn Ravensworth homestead into an open-cut coal mine. Brook Mitchell Known as the Ravensworth Homestead Complex, the site was settled by Dr James Bowman and his wife, Mary Macarthur Bowman. She had been given a generous dowry of 2000 sheep and 200 head of cattle by her parents, John and Elizabeth Macarthur. As part of her deliberations, Sharpe said she had visited Ravensworth, met with owners and local Aboriginal groups, and considered the view of the local council. When told of the decision, Laurie Perry, the chief executive of the Wonnarua Nation Aboriginal Corporation, who met with the minister, said: “Wow, that took a while.”



“So it is heritage listed, that is a good thing,” he said from his office in Singleton. Related Article Heritage Coal miner to ‘relocate’ historic homestead and Indigenous site for mine In dispute, though, is whether a massacre of 18 Indigenous people in 1826 by a posse of armed men happened on the site or in the local area. Perry, whose great-great-uncle Herbie worked for the Bowmans, said he told Sharpe the massacre happened 30 kilometres away. Scott Franks, the head of Plains Clan of the Wonnarua, told the Herald in 2021 that it was “hallowed ground” to Indigenous people.



Franks told the ABC in 2023 that a listing would be a big win. “Hopefully, we’re going to get some closure for this, and we can all get on with reconciling the issues that happened there.” A University of Newcastle database of colonial massacres says it happened near Ravensworth. Editor's pick City life Not ready to give up the Australian dream? This could be the solution Heritage NSW said Ravensworth could provide rare insights into Aboriginal history and frontier conflict, colonial building techniques, farming practices and the working lives of convicts in a non-institutional setting. There had been escalating episodes of violence “on, near, or were associated with, the estate from 1825” – starting with Aboriginal raids, the “plunder” of crops and attacks on convict workers and the murder of a hut-keeper in June 1826. This culminated in the “Ravensworth massacre” but its precise location was lacking.



NSW’s Independent Planning Commission rejected Glencore’s 2022 application to continue operating Glendell, citing Indigenous cultural values and heritage impact. Glencore has disputed the locations of the massacres of Aboriginal people. It previously offered to relocate the buildings, brick by brick. A spokesperson for Glencore said the company had no comment at this time. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Anna Wintour’s wardrobe hack is a bombshell that puts most of us to shame
World.content:
LifestyleFashionAnna Wintour Opinion Anna Wintour’s wardrobe hack is a bombshell that puts most of us to shame Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist April 24, 2026 — 11:00am

April 24, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Possibly defying both logic and fashion, my wardrobe is a massively random time capsule. There’s my nan Beatrice’s chocolate fake fur. Mum’s late ’60s aqua crocheted mini. My creepy first bra. The coat hanger from long-gone Block Arcade couturier Alouette that held the bridesmaid dress for my sister’s wedding. My wedding veil (handmade by Melbourne bridal doyenne Jane Hill back when she sewed in the front room of her house) and the dressing gown our son Felix slouched around in as a teenager. My daughter Sadie’s year 11 formal dress, a yellow and black snakeskin Cue job which I wore to ring in 2019. Anna Wintour attends the Met Gala last year. AP There are tonnes more, from pregnancy bikinis to 1990s Genki striped tops to Scanlan Theodore copper harem pants with genie-from-Aladdin energy. I love everything, even the coat hanger. Time and place and a few grass stains and a vein of Fracas perfume. And memories. Which is why I was bedazzled (it isn’t too strong a word) by a new revelation about Anna Wintour’s own wardrobe.





Based on a seven-year stint at Vogue, Fino’s insider intel has been spun into a new book, Best Dressed. Close enough to her old boss to have her at her wedding, she said Wintour sees people and things as “useful” or “noise”. Her attitude? “If there’s no purpose to it, why have it?” Every season she picks 20 looks, wears them, then gets rid of them. “Next,” says Fino. “You and I don’t replace our white T-shirts every year. Anna does.” Wintour, pictured in New York in 2019, AP That lack of sentimentality and ability to detach is fascinating to someone who thinks Marie Kondo’s decluttering gospel is a God-awful anathema to a joyful life. My one finger to Kondo includes three pregnancy tests with faded lines, tubs of loose photos of who knows what, an HSC English exam, my dead dog Maggie’s old meds and an empty bottle of Blue Grass body lotion that was on my nan Neita’s dressing table when she died in 1993.



But Wintour’s ruthless editing surfaces something that has me wondering, especially because shedding is chic. My friend Abigayle pressed jewellery on me during Friday drinks at hers: “I’m getting rid of stuff. Take it.” Related Article Opinion

Body image My husband had a chance encounter in a Vietnam hotel. Some people have an ease with their bodies Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist It’s not a question of whether nostalgia is healthy. For many of us, being able to remember the Sounds Unlimited theme or Ciak shoes isn’t trivia. It’s orientation. It’s more about whether we’re keeping objects or keeping our past selves on standby. Is there something slightly delusional about refusing to let a moment be over? Or is it really human? I mean, we live in an age of obsessive archiving. Take pictures of ice-cream cones, see every minute as worth keeping, every stop on the roadie as atmospheric and thus worth 112 photos you’ll never look at again.



And yet for all that frantic keeping, something still slips. You can have every shot from a holiday and not quite remember how it felt to be there. You can follow your kids’ whole lives on your camera roll and still be surprised by how fast it went. Maybe that’s why the coat hanger matters. The physical thing is what gets you back in the room faster than memory can. Unless you’re Anna Wintour, who keeps almost nothing and seems completely anchored anyway. I admire that. But I can’t help seeing the drape of a sleeve and feeling a pang for a great day. Kate Halfpenny is the founder of Bad Mother Media. World.title: Classical Greek set to be lone odyssey for eager Victorian students
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation Classical Greek set to be lone odyssey for eager Victorian students Caroline Schelle April 24, 2026 — 11:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

For Victorian pupils eager to study classical Greek, the path forward is a lone odyssey through the wine-dark sea, as one of the state’s final strongholds of the subject is closing its books after nearly 150 years. Xavier College in Kew confirmed this week it will end its 147-year tradition of offering the subject due to low enrolments, but insisted it would leave the door open for future students. From left: Atticus Iliou Horn, 14, Zoe Kalanis, 15, and Peter Sofiadellis, 14, all study classical Greek and were hoping to continue it into VCE, but the subject is now at risk of being dropped. PENNY STEPHENS “While Xavier has a long history of teaching classical Greek, enrolments have not been historically consistent,” a spokesman for the school confirmed to The Age. Though the four Xavier College students undertaking the subject in years 9 and 10 this year will not be able to study the subject at VCE level, the school insisted they “have not closed the door to classical Greek if student interest grows”.



Related Article Education Veni, vidi, VCE: How a dead language helps students get top marks Through Greek Community of Melbourne Schools, students from different years across the state are learning the subject. This includes 14-year-old Atticus Iliou Horn, who is taking classes privately through the organisation, and said he was drawn to the subject as he wanted to try something new. “I think it’s a shame it may not continue, since I really enjoy the subject,” he said. English and modern Greek have inherited many aspects of classical Greek, he added. His friends Peter Sofiadellis,14, and Zoe Kalanis, 15, agreed.



“We should motivate more students to do the subject, and whether that’s scaling or promoting the subject in better ways, taking the subject out of VCE isn’t really the answer,” Sofiadellis said. For Kalanis, studying classical Greek helps her understand her place in the world. “It’s important to understand the world we live in, and ancient Greek is super-duper helpful to understand, you know, the roots of our languages and deepen our connection to our own mother country and language,” she said. Despite being a “silent” language that no one speaks, “it’s still very much alive in what I’m saying right now”, Kalanis said. Though classic works like The Odyssey are reserved for university, high school students learn texts from Herodotus and Aristophanes.



Teacher Miltiadis Paikopoulos said it is unfortunately one of those subjects that “a lot of people assumed would be around forever … but it’s had these chronic problems” of low enrolment for a long time. According to figures from the Victorian Curriculum and Assessment Authority (VCAA), which develops and carries out the state’s curriculum and exams for year 11 and year 12 students, only three students were enrolled in classical Greek for year 12 last year, compared with seven in 2024, and 12 students in 2023. These teens love classical Greek but fear for its future. PENNY STEPHENS Paikopoulos said for the subject to survive, the VCAA needed to amend its exams and there needed to be more promotion of the benefits of the language. “The skills you learn from classical Greek, the standards that it imposes on students, they flow through to all of the other subjects,” he said.



“Studying ancient Greek text within the historical context also gives students something like an advantage of studying other VCE subjects, like ancient history,” he said. Another problem was, he believed, many students did not know the subject existed. “In other words, it’s a problem with accessibility.” The issue is further complicated by the fact that Victoria’s exam materials are shared with the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA), which has said it may discontinue courses. “If the course numbers increase above 15, the discontinuation process will pause,” the NESA website reads. However, if student enrolment numbers fall below 15, courses are expected to cease by 2030.



Related Article Education The unpopular VCE subjects that could face the axe Victoria has one of the largest subject offerings in the country, with 116 topics that students can complete as part of the Victorian Certificate of Education, including more than 45 languages. The resources required to maintain so many subjects has been identified as a major issue for the authority as part of a review into the VCAA. “Many of the challenges in the VCAA can, in part, be traced back to the complexity of managing such a large range and number of subjects, all requiring a significant base workload,” governance expert Dr Yehudi Blacher found in the report published last year. World.title: France ‘open’ to selling Australia submarines if AUKUS collapses
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAUKUS France ‘open’ to selling Australia submarines if AUKUS collapses Matthew Knott April 24, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

One of France’s top ministers says the country would be willing to sell submarines to Australia if the AUKUS pact collapses, despite the acrimony sparked by the cancellation of a $90 billion deal five years ago. The Morrison government ditched a contract with Naval Group, a shipbuilding firm majority-owned by the French government, in 2021 in favour of a plan to acquire nuclear-powered submarines with the United States and United Kingdom. French President Emmanuel Macron visiting a nuclear submarine base in Crozon, northwest France, last month. AP The move triggered a diplomatic rupture between the two nations, with France recalling its ambassador from Canberra and the then French foreign minister accusing Australia of a “stab in the back”. Australia later paid $835 million in compensation to Naval Group and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese travelled to Paris to mend ties with French President Emmanuel Macron.



Asked whether his nation would be willing to enter another submarine deal with Australia, French Trade Minister Nicolas Forissier said that France was “not looking at the past”. “We will, of course, always be ready to [pursue] any partnership that would answer to the needs of Australia because we’re friends,” he told reporters in Sydney. “We are open to develop any partnership because I think we, again, are very much like-minded. We have the same philosophy.” France’s foreign trade minister, Nicolas Forissier, speaking during a January television interview. Bloomberg Retired rear admiral Peter Briggs has called for Australia to ditch AUKUS and instead seek to acquire a fleet of 12 Suffren-class nuclear-powered attack submarines from Naval Group.



Briggs has argued the US will not have enough spare submarines to provide any to Australia, and that it would be more cost-effective and lower risk to acquire Suffren-class submarines given they are already in service with the French navy. Related Article Exclusive

AUKUS Australia’s depending on AUKUS Virginia-class subs. The US says they’re not its priority “It offers the solution to our AUKUS problems,” he wrote in a 2024 piece for the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. A Suffren-class submarine weighs 4600 tonnes compared to 7800 tonnes for the Virginia-class boats Australia plans to acquire from the US. It carries a crew of 65 submariners compared to around 132 for a Virginia-class submarine. The Suffren-class use low-enriched uranium fuel and needs refuelling every 10 years, whereas the US and British designs use highly enriched uranium and are intended never to be refuelled.



Forissier said the topic of submarines had not come up during his discussions in Australia, and local officials insist they are fully committed to AUKUS. Admiral Samuel Paparo, the top US military commander for the Indo-Pacific, this week told congress the AUKUS plan was “on track”, even though the US needs to turbocharge its submarine production rates. Asked at a conference last month whether it was too late to abandon AUKUS is favour of a new deal, Briggs said that “it is never too late to stop a plan that is not going to bloody work”. Senior Defence Department official Hugh Jeffrey told the same conference: “Defence has been directed to pursue AUKUS and we are pursuing AUKUS and that’s our plan. I would not venture into the space about ‘Plan B’ or ‘Plan C’.”



Jeffrey said Australia would be left without any submarines to replace the ageing Collins-class boats if political leaders again change their mind, urging everyone involved to “get on with business”. “This effort under AUKUS is the fourth, by my count, attempt to replace a submarine program that we began in the 1980s. Each effort, since then, to replace it has fallen afoul of domestic politics. Are we really thinking that this should be the fourth?” he asked. “If you really want to be in a position where we have no submarines, then turn back. ” Loading Forissier is the first European trade minister to visit the country since Australia and the European Union struck a free trade deal in late March.



He said he was hopeful Australia and France would be able to work together on critical minerals so they do not become “hostages in the future”, an allusion to China’s dominance of the key components for everything from iPhones to solar panels. Related Article AUKUS ‘Headed for a train smash’: Former commander’s dire AUKUS warning As a result of the free trade agreement’s removal of tariffs on European imports, Forissier said he expected Australians to buy more champagne and French dairy products. French consumers were also becoming more open to drinking imported Australian wine, he said. Forissier said that with global trade conditions become more “violent” and uncertain, it was important for countries such as Australia and France to work together as a force for stability.



US President Donald Trump imposes tariffs but “sometimes he forgets them two days after”, he said, referring to Trump’s shortlived threat of 200 per cent tariffs on imports on French wine and champagne when Macron declined an offer to join his ‘Board of Peace’ to oversee a post-war Gaza. World.title: ‘Wow, that took a while’: After two-year delay, verdict reached on fate of 200-year-old landmark
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWHeritage ‘Wow, that took a while’: After two-year delay, verdict reached on fate of 200-year-old landmark Julie Power April 24, 2026 — 11:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

NSW Heritage Minister Penny Sharpe has added the 200-year-old Hunter Valley sheep station Ravensworth to the state’s heritage list, despite opposition from its owner, the coal miner Glencore, and continuing debate about its contested Indigenous history. In a statement, Sharpe acknowledged her decision had taken “much longer than the statutory deadline” of two weeks. The Heritage Council recommended the listing in late 2023. The mine operations at Ravensworth in the Hunter Valley in 2021. Janie Barrett “Sometimes decisions are complex, and it is appropriate that ministers take time to consider the many facets of an issue and talk to those involved,” she said. “I note that [Glencore] do not support the listing, and they expressed this to me in person.”



Located between Singleton and Muswellbrook in the Upper Hunter, the 450-hectare site is surrounded by open-cut coal mine properties mostly owned by Glencore, including the controversial Glendell mine to the south. Scott Franks is fighting a plan to turn Ravensworth homestead into an open-cut coal mine. Brook Mitchell Known as the Ravensworth Homestead Complex, the site was settled by Dr James Bowman and his wife, Mary Macarthur Bowman. She had been given a generous dowry of 2000 sheep and 200 head of cattle by her parents, John and Elizabeth Macarthur. As part of her deliberations, Sharpe said she had visited Ravensworth, met with owners and local Aboriginal groups, and considered the view of the local council. When told of the decision, Laurie Perry, the chief executive of the Wonnarua Nation Aboriginal Corporation, who met with the minister, said: “Wow, that took a while.”



“So it is heritage listed, that is a good thing,” he said from his office in Singleton. Related Article Heritage Coal miner to ‘relocate’ historic homestead and Indigenous site for mine In dispute, though, is whether a massacre of 18 Indigenous people in 1826 by a posse of armed men happened on the site or in the local area. Perry, whose great-great-uncle Herbie worked for the Bowmans, said he told Sharpe the massacre happened 30 kilometres away. Scott Franks, the head of Plains Clan of the Wonnarua, told the Herald in 2021 that it was “hallowed ground” to Indigenous people.



Franks told the ABC in 2023 that a listing would be a big win. “Hopefully, we’re going to get some closure for this, and we can all get on with reconciling the issues that happened there.” A University of Newcastle database of colonial massacres says it happened near Ravensworth. Editor's pick City life Not ready to give up the Australian dream? This could be the solution Heritage NSW said Ravensworth could provide rare insights into Aboriginal history and frontier conflict, colonial building techniques, farming practices and the working lives of convicts in a non-institutional setting. There had been escalating episodes of violence “on, near, or were associated with, the estate from 1825” – starting with Aboriginal raids, the “plunder” of crops and attacks on convict workers and the murder of a hut-keeper in June 1826. This culminated in the “Ravensworth massacre” but its precise location was lacking.



NSW’s Independent Planning Commission rejected Glencore’s 2022 application to continue operating Glendell, citing Indigenous cultural values and heritage impact. Glencore has disputed the locations of the massacres of Aboriginal people. It previously offered to relocate the buildings, brick by brick. A spokesperson for Glencore said the company had no comment at this time. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
